issues.legal_issue: Membership in a particular religious school does not, by itself, require worship to occur only in a private temple.
material_facts: The temple was associated with a religious school whose followers were said to worship through an Acharya in his residence.
The appellant argued that the school’s tenets prohibited public worship, but did not press that contention after the Court’s earlier decision on the same subject was cited.
issues.conclusion: There is no general rule that the religious school prohibits public temples; whether a particular temple is public depends on its facts.
issues.legal_principle: In Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan, the Court held that neither the tenets nor religious practices of the Vallabha school necessarily require worship in a private temple. The character of each temple must be decided on the relevant facts.

predicates.temple_status_is_at_issue: The proceeding requires the court to determine whether a temple is public or private.
predicates.followers_belong_to_a_religious_school: The people associated with worship at the temple follow a particular religious school.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a temple associated with followers of a religious school, their membership in that school alone does not make the temple private.

issues.legal_issue: A temple of unknown or ancient origin is public when the evidence of its use, support, and treatment establishes public worship as of right.
material_facts: The temple’s origin could not be established with certainty and was treated as lost in antiquity.
Followers regularly worshipped there as of right and participated in its ceremonies and festivals.
Devotees made gifts and contributions, and the temple was substantially maintained from those contributions.
Separate accounts and documents treated the deity and temple as distinct from the religious head and his personal affairs.
The temple’s management and devotees treated it as public; the building’s residential appearance did not alter that conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The temple was a public temple.
issues.legal_principle: The issue is a mixed question of law and fact. If a temple is shown to have originated as public, nothing further is needed to establish its public character; if its origin is private, unknown, or lost in antiquity, public use and other circumstances must be considered. Relevant factors include origin, management, gifts and contributions, rights exercised by worshippers, and the understanding of the manager and devotees. Public worship as of right is strong evidence, and public offerings and contributions may support a presumption of public character. The Court relied on Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan; Lakshmana v. Subramania; Mundancheri Koman v. Achutan Nair; Deoki Nandan v. Murlidar; and Narayan Bhagwant Rao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayak Gosavi.

rule.if: proceeding_determines_whether_a_temple_is_public and temple_origin_is_unknown_or_ancient and worshippers_use_temple_as_of_right and public_contributions_support_temple

predicates.proceeding_determines_whether_a_temple_i: The proceeding requires a decision on whether a temple is public or private.
predicates.temple_origin_is_unknown_or_ancient: The temple’s origin is unknown, lost in antiquity, or not established as private.
predicates.worshippers_use_temple_as_of_right: Members of the public or a section of it regularly worship at the temple as of right.
predicates.public_contributions_support_temple: Devotees make offerings or contributions that support the temple and its activities.

issues.definition: Where a proceeding concerns a temple of unknown or ancient origin, public worship as of right together with public financial support establishes that the temple is public.

issues.legal_issue: Properties shown by the evidence to have been acquired, maintained, or treated for the temple belong to the temple rather than to its religious head personally.
material_facts: Separate accounts were maintained for the temple and the religious head, and the evidence showed that the temple received gifts and contributions and had resources for acquisitions.
The properties were recorded, used, or accounted for as temple property, and some had been expressly gifted or purchased for the temple.
The religious head failed to produce some relevant accounts and documents, and documents produced were found to have been altered or tampered with.
The appellant did not establish that the properties were her personal property.
issues.conclusion: All the properties listed in the suit schedules were properties of the temple.
issues.legal_principle: The ownership of religious endowment property is determined from the evidence, including the source of acquisition, gifts, accounts, records, use, and the manner in which the property was dealt with. The Court accepted an adverse inference from the deliberate non-production of relevant accounts and documents and relied on the distinction between temple and personal accounts. The principles concerning public and private endowments in Deoki Nandan v. Murlidar and Mundancheri Koman v. Achutan Nair informed the Court’s assessment.

predicates.proceeding_determines_temple_property_ow: The proceeding requires a decision whether disputed properties belong to a temple or its manager personally.
predicates.temple_and_manager_have_separate_account: Separate accounts are maintained for the temple’s affairs and the manager’s personal affairs.
predicates.properties_are_acquired_or_treated_for_t: The properties are acquired with temple resources, dedicated to the temple, used for temple purposes, or consistently recorded and managed as temple property.
predicates.manager_does_not_establish_personal_owne: The manager does not establish that the disputed properties are personal property.

issues.definition: In a proceeding over temple property, properties acquired or consistently treated for the temple belong to it when the manager’s separate accounts and lack of proof of personal ownership support that conclusion.

issues.legal_issue: A new factual theory inconsistent with the pleaded case need not be entertained for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The written defence asserted that the properties were the religious head’s personal property and denied that any dedication or trust existed.
In the Supreme Court, the appellant advanced a different factual theory that some properties had been dedicated to a private trust.
The new theory depended on factual matters about dedication and the accounts, rather than being a purely legal contention.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the new factual plea.
issues.legal_principle: A party cannot replace its pleaded factual case with a materially inconsistent factual theory at a later stage when that theory depends on facts the party knew or should have addressed. The Court rejected the argument that the new theory was purely legal because it essentially raised questions of fact.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The court is considering a party’s appeal from a lower-court decision.
predicates.new_factual_theory_is_inconsistent_with_: The party advances a factual case on appeal that materially differs from the case set out in its pleadings.
predicates.theory_depends_on_untried_facts: The new theory requires factual determinations that were not presented and tried as part of the pleaded case.

issues.definition: On appeal, a materially inconsistent factual theory that depends on facts not tried as part of the pleaded case is not entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A religious head may use temple income for reasonable personal and family maintenance after the temple’s primary needs are met.
material_facts: The religious head had an important religious role in the temple and was not merely a manager.
The temple income was primarily required for worship, festivals, upkeep, renovation, and improvement of the temple.
The plaintiffs conceded that, subject to those requirements, the religious head could use temple income for reasonable maintenance of himself and his family.
issues.conclusion: The religious head may use temple income for his and his family’s reasonably comfortable maintenance, subject to meeting the temple’s primary needs.
issues.legal_principle: In temples of the religious school, the religious head has an important religious position. Temple income must first meet the expenses of worship and festivals and the upkeep, renovation, and improvement of the premises; subject to those demands, the religious head may use income for reasonable maintenance of himself and his family.

predicates.temple_has_a_religious_head_with_an_inst: The temple has a religious head who holds an important role in its religious life.
predicates.temple_needs_have_priority: Income is required first for worship, festivals, and the upkeep and improvement of the temple.
predicates.income_remains_after_temple_needs: Some temple income remains after the temple’s primary requirements are met.

issues.definition: When a religious head has an institutional role, temple needs are met first, and income remains, the remainder may be used for reasonable maintenance of the head and family.
